title: Backpropagation, 1986, derived rather than memorised
story:
The problem is credit assignment. A network with intermediate layers produces a wrong answer, and the question is how much a particular weight several layers back contributed to that error. The obvious way to find out is to nudge the weight and see what changes — but that costs a full forward pass per weight, and there are millions of weights, so the obvious way is not available.

Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams published Learning representations by back-propagating errors in Nature on 9 October 1986. Their description is worth having in their own words, because it says what the result is about: the procedure repeatedly adjusts the weights of connections so as to minimise a measure of the difference between the actual output vector of the net and the desired output vector, and as a result of the weight adjustments internal hidden units which are not part of the input or output come to represent important features of the task domain.

That second clause is the claim that mattered. Not that gradients can be computed efficiently — that the hidden units, left to themselves, come to represent something. Learned representations, rather than an optimisation trick, is what the paper was announcing.

Which matters because the method itself is older, and the usual telling attributes it to this paper. Seppo Linnainmaa introduced the reverse mode of automatic differentiation in his 1970 master's thesis, without reference to neural networks, publishing in English in 1976. Paul Werbos's 1974 Harvard doctoral thesis described how reverse mode differentiation could train neural networks, which is the first application of the method to this problem. It was then reinvented several times, including by Parker in 1985, before the 1986 paper brought it to general attention.

So the accurate sentence is that 1986 is when backpropagation started to matter, not when it was invented. Priority here is genuinely disputed — different accounts weight the general method, its first application to networks, and the demonstration that made the field pay attention differently, and reasonable people land in different places. What is not in dispute is that the 1986 authors were not the first, and a lesson that says they invented it is repeating a convenient simplification.

Now the mechanism, which is the part worth being able to derive rather than recall. Every operation in the network is a function with a known local derivative. The chain rule says the derivative of a composition is the product of the local derivatives along the path. So once the error at the output is known, each node's contribution can be computed from the contribution of the nodes it feeds and its own local derivative — which is a single quantity multiplied by a single quantity, per edge, sweeping backwards. Every gradient in the network, in one pass.

The reason it is the reverse direction specifically is a cost argument, and it is the thing to actually understand. Forward accumulation computes the derivatives of all outputs with respect to one input per sweep, so its cost scales with the number of inputs. Reverse accumulation computes the derivatives of one output with respect to all inputs per sweep, so its cost scales with the number of outputs. Training has one scalar loss and millions of parameters — one output, an enormous number of inputs — so reverse accumulation is a single sweep where forward accumulation would be millions. The asymmetry is entirely about the shape of the problem, and for a problem with one input and many outputs the preference reverses.

The bill is memory, and it is stated far less often than the speed. The costs of forward activation spreading essentially equal the costs of backward derivative calculation, which is the good news — but the backward sweep needs the intermediate values the forward pass produced, so they must all be retained until it runs. That is why training a model takes so much more memory than running one, and why memory rather than arithmetic is what bounds the size of model a given machine can train.

worked.problem: What is the difference between forward and reverse accumulation, and why does training use reverse?
worked.reasoning:
Both compute exact derivatives by applying the chain rule to the same computation; they differ in the direction the products are accumulated, and that direction decides the cost.

Forward accumulation propagates derivatives with respect to one chosen input alongside the computation itself. One sweep gives you the derivatives of every output with respect to that one input, so covering all inputs costs one sweep per input — cost scales with the number of inputs.

Reverse accumulation runs the computation first, then sweeps backwards from one chosen output. One sweep gives the derivative of that output with respect to every input, so cost scales with the number of outputs.

Training has one scalar loss and millions of parameters. That is one output and an enormous number of inputs, which is exactly the shape reverse accumulation suits: one backward sweep yields every parameter's gradient, where forward accumulation would need a sweep per parameter. That is the entire argument, and it is worth noticing that it is about the problem's shape rather than about one method being better — for a function with one input and many outputs, the preference reverses.

Mechanically it is simpler than its reputation. Every operation has a known local derivative, and the chain rule makes the derivative of a composition the product of local derivatives along the path. So each node's gradient is computed from the gradients of the nodes it feeds and its own local derivative: one multiplication and one accumulation per edge, sweeping backwards from the loss. Every gradient in the network in a single pass.

The cost worth stating, because the speed gets all the attention: the costs of forward activation spreading essentially equal the costs of backward derivative calculation, so a training step is roughly twice an inference step in arithmetic. But the backward sweep consumes the intermediate values the forward pass produced, so all of them must be retained until it runs. That is why training a model takes far more memory than running one, and why memory rather than arithmetic bounds the size of model a machine can train.

I would also correct the attribution, since it is usually given as a 1986 invention. The Nature paper of 9 October 1986 is when it started to matter, not when it was invented: Linnainmaa introduced the reverse mode in his 1970 master's thesis without reference to neural networks, Werbos's 1974 Harvard thesis first applied it to training them, and it was reinvented several times including by Parker in 1985. Priority is genuinely disputed — accounts weight the general method, its first application to networks, and the demonstration that made the field notice differently — but that the 1986 authors were not first is not in dispute.

And what their paper actually claimed is more interesting than efficient gradients anyway: that as a result of the weight adjustments, internal hidden units which are not part of the input or output come to represent important features of the task domain. Learned representations. That is the announcement, and the gradient method was how they got there.

problem.practice: Implement the backward pass for a single multiplication node and a single addition node by hand, then chain three of them. Once you have seen that each node needs only its own local derivative and the gradient arriving from above, the rest of the algorithm is bookkeeping.

beats.broke: A network with intermediate layers had no way to assign responsibility for an output error to a weight several layers back, and measuring each weight's effect by perturbing it costs one forward pass per weight.
beats.fix: Apply the chain rule in reverse across the computation, accumulating the derivative of one scalar output with respect to every intermediate quantity in a single backward sweep.
beats.cost: The whole forward computation must be retained for the backward sweep to consume, which is why memory rather than arithmetic bounds how large a model can be trained.

interview.q: What is the difference between forward and reverse accumulation, and why does training use reverse?
interview.trap: Treating reverse as intrinsically superior. The advantage comes from the problem having one output and many inputs — with one input and many outputs the preference reverses.
interview.answer:
Both compute exact derivatives by applying the chain rule to the same computation, differing in the direction the products accumulate — and that direction sets the cost.

Forward accumulation propagates derivatives with respect to one chosen input alongside the computation, so one sweep gives every output's derivative with respect to that input, and cost scales with the number of inputs. Reverse accumulation runs the computation, then sweeps back from one chosen output, giving that output's derivative with respect to every input, so cost scales with the number of outputs.

Training has one scalar loss and millions of parameters — one output, an enormous number of inputs — so one backward sweep yields every gradient where forward would need one per parameter. That is the whole argument, and it rests on the shape of the problem rather than on one method being better: with one input and many outputs the preference reverses.

Mechanically it is simpler than its reputation: every operation has a known local derivative, and each node's gradient is the gradients of the nodes it feeds times its own local derivative — one multiply and one accumulate per edge, sweeping back from the loss.

The cost worth stating is memory. The backward sweep costs roughly what the forward pass costs in arithmetic, but it consumes the intermediate values the forward pass produced, so all of them must be retained. That is why training takes far more memory than inference and why memory rather than arithmetic bounds trainable model size.

I would also correct the attribution, since this is usually given as a 1986 invention. The Nature paper of 9 October 1986 is when it started to matter, not when it was invented: Linnainmaa introduced the reverse mode in a 1970 master's thesis without reference to neural networks, Werbos's 1974 Harvard thesis first applied it to training them, and it was reinvented several times including by Parker in 1985. Priority is genuinely disputed, but that the 1986 authors were not first is not.

And their actual claim is more interesting than efficient gradients: that as a result of the weight adjustments, internal hidden units which are not part of the input or output come to represent important features of the task domain. Learned representations were the announcement.
